title: Lazarus at the gate (Luke 16:19–31)
hook: a rich man never noticed the beggar at his own gate

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crooked steward used his last afternoon to make friends with his master's money. Your line was god or mammon.

Things right at your door can become invisible exactly because they're always there: the recycling bin, the neighbor's car, maybe a person sitting against the wall of the corner store you pass every day. Jesus tells a parable about two men separated by a single gate. One lives behind it in luxury. The other lies just outside it, every day. One of them has a name in the story. It's not the rich one.
screen: `WHAT'S OUTSIDE YOUR FRONT DOOR?` → `ALWAYS THERE, SO INVISIBLE.` → `TWO MEN, ONE GATE.`

segments.voice: Luke paints the rich man in two strokes: clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting sumptuously every day. Purple dye was ruinously expensive, the color of kings. Then the other man: "And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores." He longs for the crumbs from the table, and the dogs come and lick his sores. Of all the people Jesus invents for his parables, Lazarus is the only one given a name. Abraham and Moses appear here too, but they come from Scripture. Later Latin readers called the rich man Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's bosom. The rich man is in torment, and now he looks up and sees Lazarus. He knows his name. He knew it all along. He asks Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water, as if Lazarus were still a servant. Abraham answers gently, calling him son, and says a great chaos is now fixed between them. One more request: send Lazarus to warn my five brothers. Abraham says: they have Moses and the prophets. Let them hear them. If they won't, they won't believe even if someone rises from the dead. The rich man is never accused of hurting Lazarus, never cruel to him. His sin is simpler and more common: Lazarus was at his gate every day, and he stepped around him. The chasm after death is just the gate made permanent.
screen: `PURPLE AND FINE LINEN.` · `THE ONLY NAMED MAN JESUS INVENTS.` · `HE KNEW HIS NAME ALL ALONG.` · `THE GATE MADE PERMANENT.` · then, large: `A BEGGAR, NAMED LAZARUS, AT HIS GATE.`

segments.voice: Walk in your mind along the route you take every day, front door, street, store, office, the screen you scroll, and ask who is there every day that you've stopped seeing. Let one person come into focus: someone sitting outside, a lonely neighbor, a coworker who eats alone. If you pray, pray for them, by name if you know it.
Lazarus. The poor man with a name, lying every day at the door of a rich man who stepped around him. Today's word.
Your line: he was at the gate. Every day, a name, right there. Day four hundred seventy-two, in the books.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich man and Lazarus at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and popes, Paul VI and Francis among them, have used it to speak about the rich and the poor in today's world.

chat.meaning: The rich man is never accused of cruelty; his sin was simpler: Lazarus lay at his gate every day, and he stepped around him.

sources.quoted: And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 16:20 and 'great chaos' in 16:26.

Lazarus as the only named character in Jesus' parables: a standard observation, softened to 'the only one Jesus invents' because Abraham and Moses are also named in this story. A few readers argue this is not a parable at all (Luke does not call it one); confirm framing.
'Dives' as a later name from the Latin adjective (Vulgate 'homo quidam erat dives'): confirm.
howItsDone: popes using this parable for rich and poor nations (e.g., Paul VI, Populorum Progressio 47; Francis, Lenten message 2017): confirm before keeping.
